newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Workers at Romania's Tarom may strike over changes.
newsitem.headline: Workers at Romania's Tarom may strike over changes.

text.p: Workers at Romania's state airline Tarom SA on Tuesday threatened to go on strike and ground flights unless the government revised plans to restructure the airline, cut jobs and sell Soviet-made planes.
"The restructuring plan is not viable. We can't accept it," Tarom trade union leader Romeo Iordanescu told reporters. "We are determined to strike if the minister does not reconsider."
Tarom officials were unavailable to comment.

On Monday, Transport Minister Traian Basescu said Tarom would undergo a fast restructuring programme, including layoffs and sale of its outdated Soviet-made Ilyushin-62, IL-18 and Tupolev-154 aircraft. Most of the staff involved in their maintenance would be sacked, he said.
Fresh talks between the State Ownership Fund, Tarom's majority stockholder, and the trade union on restructuring were expected on Wednesday, a company source said.

The labour protests underscored Tarom's financial problems in recent years. Saddled with huge debts, it had become clear the airline had little chance of survival without a serious bailout. Tarom's internal debts total 80 billion lei and external debts $15.5 million, according to local media reports.
Iordanescu said the ministry's plan had failed to tackle "real issues", including high fees it has to pay to air traffic control, handling and catering services.
"These fees make up 60 percent of the ticket price. This is absurd," said Alexandru Mirica, another union leader. "We want to get back the ground and fuelling services."
He accused private firms currently operating the services of monopolistic practices.
"They have no competition so they can ask for whatever fees they want. For instance, they charge an extra $100 per tonne of fuel, which is more than elsewhere in the world," he said.

Mirica said the trade union had asked management to use Soviet-made aicraft for chartered flights in the vast market of the former Soviet Union, Asia and Africa, where there were no restrictions on safety and noise.
"We have huge amounts of spare parts for the Soviet planes. Why should we turn them into scrap iron?," he said.

Under the ministry plan, Tarom would continue to use eight Antonov-24s on domestic routes along with two recently acquired Franco-Italian ATR aircraft. International routes are served by two A-310 Airbus planes, five Boeing 737s and six BAC 1-11 aircraft.
A project to buy eight Boeing 737s Next Generation was suspended last month when the Finance Ministry failed to guarantee the planned purchase. ($=7,195 lei)
